reasons: The group type list is empty, so any rule that reaches the membership check throws.
The stored policy is parsed without error handling.

terms.meaning: access control list, a record of who may do what
extra labels stored alongside a file
the user who controls the file
a right to read or to write
a fixed list of named choices

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and policy label
sections.what: Brings in the storage file type and sets the metadata label under which the access policy is kept.
sections.why: Gives one fixed place to save the policy.
sections.watch_out: Renaming this label makes existing files look as if they have no policy, so they become private.

sections.name: ObjectAccessGroupType
sections.title: Access group type list
sections.what: Declares the kinds of groups a rule can refer to, written as comments (user list, email domain, group member, subscriber). The list itself is empty.
sections.why: Likely reason: a placeholder for group kinds to be added later.
sections.watch_out: Because the list is empty, no rule can name a valid group type.

sections.name: ObjectAccessGroup
sections.title: Access group description
sections.what: Describes a group by its type and an identifier. Comments explain what the identifier means for each type.
sections.why: Reason not stated beyond defining the target of an access rule.
sections.watch_out: The identifier means something different for each type, so a rule must match its type.

sections.name: ObjectPermission
sections.title: Permission levels
sections.what: Defines two levels: read and write.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code; a basic permission model.
sections.watch_out: Read and write are separate levels, so a read grant does not allow changes.

sections.name: ObjectAclRule
sections.title: One access rule
sections.what: Pairs a group with a permission level, meaning members of that group receive that level.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: ObjectAclPolicy
sections.title: Full access policy
sections.what: The saved policy: an owner, public or private visibility, and a list of rules. It is stored as text on the file.
sections.why: Keeps access information with the file itself.
sections.watch_out: Because the policy is stored as text, any manual edit to the metadata must keep valid format or reads will fail.

sections.name: isPermissionAllowed
sections.title: Permission matching
sections.what: Decides whether a granted level covers a requested one. A read request is met by a read or write grant, while a write request is met only by a write grant.
sections.why: Lets a write grant also allow reading.

sections.name: BaseObjectAccessGroup
sections.title: Shared base for group checks
sections.what: An abstract base that requires each group type to say whether a given user is a member.
sections.why: Gives every group type the same membership check.
sections.watch_out: No group type inherits from this base yet, so it has no effect in use.

sections.name: createObjectAccessGroup
sections.title: Group factory with no types
sections.what: Turns a rule's group description into a working membership checker based on its type. Currently every type falls through to an error.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It is a placeholder, with examples in the comments.
sections.watch_out: Any rule that reaches this point throws an error, and this file does not catch it.

sections.name: setObjectAclPolicy
sections.title: Saves the access policy
sections.what: Stores a policy on a file as text in the file's metadata, after confirming the file exists. It throws if the file is missing.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the policy with the file so no separate table is needed.
sections.watch_out: The whole policy is replaced each time, so simultaneous edits can overwrite each other.

sections.name: getObjectAclPolicy
sections.title: Reads the access policy
sections.what: Reads the stored policy text from the file's metadata and turns it back into a policy, or returns nothing when none is stored.
sections.watch_out: Text that is not valid JSON makes this function throw instead of returning nothing.

sections.name: canAccessObject
sections.title: Decides whether a user may access a file
sections.what: The main gatekeeper. It denies when there is no policy. Public files can be read by anyone. Otherwise it requires a user ID, allows the owner, then checks each rule's group and permission. Anything else is denied.
sections.why: Keeps every access decision in one place.
sections.watch_out: Reaching a rule with an unknown group type throws an error instead of denying, so an access check can fail with a server error.

summary: Controls who may read or write each stored file, based on an access policy saved with that file.
why: Likely reason: files need per-owner and per-group access without a separate table. The comments suggest the group design is meant to be extended later.
how: 1. Stores the access policy as text on the file. 2. Reads it back when a check is made. 3. Lets anyone read a public file. 4. Requires a user ID for anything else. 5. Allows the owner. 6. Goes through each access rule and asks its group whether the user is a member. 7. Denies by default.
inputs: The file object, the requested permission (read or write) and the user ID if known.
outputs: A yes or no answer, or a saved policy attached to a file.
risks: No group types are defined, so any rule that reaches the membership check throws an error instead of answering. Public files can be read by anyone with no login. The policy is parsed without error handling, so damaged text throws.
debug: If a private file returns server errors, look for Unknown access group type in the logs, which points to an access rule. If a public file is unexpectedly readable, check its visibility setting. If a file is denied, check that it has a policy at all, because a missing policy means denied.
